hops.afterHeading: Adding inputs in time and in space
hops.title: Why a faint star fades when you look straight at it
hops.text: On a clear night, find a faint star and look straight at it. It often fades. Shift your gaze a little to one side and it comes back. The very center of the fovea has cones and no rods, so in light too dim for cones it leaves a blind patch about one degree across. Just off center, rods take over, and their signals converge: one model estimates that at peak about 53 rods feed through 4 rod bipolar cells and a single amacrine cell, relaying mostly via cone bipolar cells to 2 ganglion cells. Pooling many rods makes faint light easier to see, at the cost of fine detail.

sources.citation: Kalloniates M & Luu C, Light and Dark Adaptation, Webvision (University of Utah)
McKyton A, Elul D & Levin N, iScience 27(2):108929 (2024)
Dey A, Zele AJ, Feigl B & Adhikari P, Vision Research 180:1-10 (2021)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student outdoors at night, seen from behind, looking slightly to one side of a faint star.
image.caption: Looking slightly aside puts dim starlight on rods, whose pooled signals make faint light easier to see.

hops.afterHeading: When GABA pushes up: timing and site
hops.title: How nerve injury flips a spinal pain brake
hops.text: The potassium-chloride cotransporter KCC2 pumps chloride out of neurons, which helps inhibitory synapses keep them from firing. In 2003, Jeffrey Coull, Yves De Koninck and colleagues studied rats after a peripheral nerve injury. Neurons in lamina I of the spinal dorsal horn, one of the main routes carrying pain signals up to the brain, had reduced their KCC2 expression. With less chloride pumped out, the anion gradient shifted, and synaptic currents that normally inhibit these neurons became excitatory, driving their firing up. The team then blocked or knocked down spinal KCC2 in uninjured rats, and that change alone markedly lowered the threshold at which they showed a pain response.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A white laboratory rat sitting calmly on a wire-mesh platform in a tidy lab room.
image.caption: In uninjured rats, blocking or reducing spinal KCC2 alone was enough to lower the threshold for a pain response.

hops.title: Filming a lobster's stomach teeth in two chewing modes
hops.text: Lobsters chew with three teeth inside the stomach, a middle one and two serrated side ones, driven by a circuit in the thirty-neuron stomatogastric ganglion. Cut off from their usual modulatory input in a lab dish, those neurons fall silent or fire steadily with no rhythm. In 1988, Hans-Georg Heinzel slipped an endoscope down the esophagus of restrained lobsters to film the teeth. A low dose of the neuromodulator proctolin in the circulation brought on squeeze mode, all three teeth pressing together. A higher dose brought on cut-and-grind mode, with the side teeth grinding backward along the middle one. One injection kept the chewing going for 2 to 30 minutes.

sources.citation: Selverston A et al., Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences 860:35-50 (1998)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A reddish-brown lobster in a laboratory seawater tank with a thin cable coiled on the bench beside it.
image.caption: Two doses of the same neuromodulator brought on two different chewing patterns in a lobster's stomach.
